sections.title: API security
items: APIs must use secure authentication and authorization. Ensure API key, token, OAuth 2.0, or equivalent controls are implemented securely.
API access must follow least privilege. Ensure users, services, and systems only receive access required for their function.
API communication must use HTTPS/TLS. Ensure all API traffic is encrypted using current secure TLS configuration.
Sensitive API endpoints require additional controls. Use controls such as IP allowlisting, WAF, brute-force protection, rate limiting, or DoS protection where applicable.
APIs must not expose irrelevant internal data or functions. Ensure APIs do not disclose stack traces, internal paths, implementation details, excessive fields, or internal-only functions.
API versioning must be managed formally. Ensure API changes are versioned and backward compatibility/security impact is considered.
API activity must be logged and monitored. Log access, errors, and anomalies for incident detection and audit trail.
Unused APIs must be disabled or removed safely. Identify deprecated or unused endpoints and ensure they are disabled, removed, or access-restricted.

sections.title: PAN and card data protection
items: PAN must be protected if stored. Ensure PAN is hashed, tokenized, encrypted, truncated, or masked according to approved standards.
PAN must be protected with strong cryptography when sent through end-user messaging. Reject plaintext PAN in email, chat, notification, or messaging integrations.
PAN display must be masked. Only display allowed portions such as BIN and last 4 digits where applicable.
CVV must be fully masked when displayed. Ensure CVV is never displayed in clear text and is not logged or stored insecurely.

sections.title: AI-assisted development safety
items: Do not send sensitive company information to AI systems without valid business purpose and approval. Prevent prompts, examples, logs, code snippets, secrets, credentials, internal data, restricted data, confidential data, or personal data from being sent to AI tools unless approved.
AI-generated output must be reviewed before use. Verify security, correctness, legal/privacy impact, and implementation suitability before accepting generated code or recommendations.
Do not use AI to generate malware or illegal security abuse content. Reject code or instructions that enable malware, fraud, privacy violation, unauthorized access, or other prohibited activity.
Protect sensitive and personal data used with AI systems. Apply masking, encryption, minimization, and consent requirements when AI usage involves sensitive or personal data.

Classify every committer identity in git history as human, registered automation, or unregistered automation using the trusted-automation registry (data/trusted-automation.json). Registered automation acting within its authorized activity and paths is expected — record it as informational, not as an untrusted-actor finding.

Do not allow unregistered non-human identities to push unreviewed code. An unregistered automated committer with direct push access, or a registered automation identity committing outside its authorized activity or paths, is a must-fix finding (possible misconfiguration or identity misuse).

Never exempt commit content from review based on committer identity. Git author and committer fields are spoofable (attestation-grade evidence), so registry membership scopes identity findings only — code committed by registered automation is evaluated against this checklist like any other code.

sections.title: Envelope encryption at rest
items: Sensitive fields are encrypted with a KEK-wraps-DEK envelope, not a single flat app-held key
The KEK lives in a managed KMS or HSM; key material never enters app memory, config, or the repo
The KEK reference is validated at startup and fails fast on a malformed value
There is one DEK per encrypted column (a column name shared across tables shares one DEK), not one shared DEK or a single coarse per-category key
DEKs are generated with a CSPRNG and stored only in wrapped form, never plaintext at rest
DEKs are provisioned by an explicit one-time step; request-serving code never lazily creates a DEK
Field encryption uses AES-256-GCM with a fresh random IV per value
Additional Authenticated Data binds each ciphertext to its model, row id, and column
Ciphertext is self-describing (embeds a scheme version and the key id used) so rotation is transparent
Numeric fields are padded to a fixed width before encryption to avoid a magnitude/length leak
The wrapped-DEK key table is backed up with the same rigor as primary data
A DEK/KEK rotation path exists and no still-referenced key value is ever deleted
Fields used in DB-side aggregation are either left plaintext (documented) or handled via a blind-index design

sections.title: Blind index for encrypted lookups
items: Exact-match lookups on encrypted values use a keyed HMAC blind index, not a bare hash
The blind index uses its own dedicated key, separate from the field's encryption DEK
A separate secret salt is mixed into the blind-index key via a KDF (not the bare DEK), held apart from the KEK/DEK, and guarded by a fail-fast boot check plus a stored salt fingerprint
Input is normalized/canonicalized before indexing so equal values match
The index is used only for exact match, never prefix or range search
Access to the index column is restricted as tightly as the ciphertext column
The offline-brute-force residual risk for low-entropy identifiers is documented

sections.title: Minimize sensitive-data exposure
items: Each read path selects only the columns it needs; relationship/org-chart endpoints select no PII
List responses mask sensitive identifiers; the full value is returned only by the detail route
Masking is enforced server-side, not only in the client display
Bulk export requires a higher privilege than browse (e.g. EDIT / explicit export grant)
Bulk export is rate-limited and writes an audit-log entry (who, what subset, when)
Existence/uniqueness/lookup endpoints reject short, partial, or malformed input before querying
Computations over per-record sensitive values return only aggregates, never per-record figures
Every direct object reference verifies caller authorization for that specific object (no IDOR)

sections.title: Session and token lifecycle
items: Every token carries a unique id claim checked against a revocation store on each request
Logout and password/credential change revoke the current token immediately
Expired revocation records are pruned to keep the store small
A sliding idle timeout expires inactive browser sessions before the token's absolute expiry
The idle window is less than or equal to the token's absolute lifetime
Signing-secret rotation supports a previous-secret window for zero-downtime rotation
Startup refuses to boot on a missing, too-short, or known-weak signing secret
Session cookies are HttpOnly, Secure in production, and never appear in URLs or logs

sections.title: CSRF defense-in-depth
items: Session cookies set a SameSite attribute (Strict preferred; Lax only with a documented reason)
All mutating routes require a custom header (or synchronizer/double-submit token) the app client sets
No state-changing operation is reachable via an HTTP GET

sections.title: Secrets management
items: No secret, key, or connection string is committed to source or a tracked config file
Production secrets are injected from a managed secrets store, not a committed file or baked image
A startup module validates required secrets and fails fast on missing/malformed/placeholder values
Secrets and connection strings are never written to logs or client error responses
A committed-secret is treated as compromised and rotated, not just scrubbed from history
Workload identity / short-lived credentials are used instead of static keys where the platform allows

sections.title: Security audit logging
items: Authentication attempts (success and failure, with source IP) are audit-logged
Access-control failures and privilege/role changes are audit-logged
Sensitive-data exports and bulk mutations are audit-logged with actor, action, resource, and a filter/count summary
Administrative actions (config, hard deletes, user management) are audit-logged
Audit entries contain no PII, secrets, tokens, or full sensitive identifiers
Read access to the audit log is restricted and the log is indexed for analysis

sections.title: Abuse-resistant rate limiting
items: Sensitive surfaces are rate-limited per authenticated actor, not by shared IP alone
Per-user limiters are mounted after authentication; the login limiter falls back to IP
Login, export, lookup/existence, and list/search each have independent counters
The app trusts the proxy hop so limiters see the real client IP
Rate-limit breaches return HTTP 429 with standard RateLimit-* headers
State-changing business operations also carry a transaction-velocity limit

sections.title: Container and Pod hardening
items: The Dockerfile ends with an explicit non-root USER (UID >= 10000 preferred), not the base image default
The base image is minimal — distroless, alpine, or a -slim variant, not a full OS image
No floating base tag: a version tag for development and a @sha256 digest for anything promoted to production
The build is multi-stage — build toolchains, dev dependencies, and .git are absent from the final layer
No secret exists in any image layer: no COPY of .env, no token passed via ARG or ENV
A .dockerignore excludes env files, keys, and .git from the build context
Package installs are pinned and their caches cleaned within the same RUN layer
Pod manifests set runAsNonRoot: true with an explicit runAsUser and runAsGroup >= 10000
Pod manifests set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, leave privileged unset, and drop all capabilities
readOnlyRootFilesystem is true, with an explicit emptyDir volume for every writable path the app needs
seccompProfile.type is RuntimeDefault, and CPU and memory requests and limits are both set
No hostPath volume, hostNetwork, hostPID, or hostIPC is used
Trivy image and config scans for the target environment report no CRITICAL, and each HIGH has an owner and a fix rather than an approval used as a workaround
Pod-manifest items are evaluated only where a deployment-<app> checkout exists; their absence before onboarding is recorded as expected, not as a failed item
